RotatE uses normalized weights w_j=softmax(αs_j), detached during backpropagation, on negative logistic losses. The negative-score gradient is proportional to w_jσ(s_j): increasing temperature concentrates updates on the highest-scoring negatives, potentially amplifying false negatives. Normalization fixes total weight, but permits one extreme negative to dominate; detachment removes gradients through weight construction, not this concentration. [Official implementation](https://github.com/DeepGraphLearning/KnowledgeGraphEmbedding/blob/master/codes/model.py).

Hard-BPR (2024) instead changes the pairwise loss: −log[(σ(cx+b)+a)/(1+a)], x=s_positive−s_negative. For a>0, its gradient magnitude cσ(cx+b)[1−σ(cx+b)]/[σ(cx+b)+a] vanishes at both extremes, emphasizing an intermediate margin range. This is actual suppression of extremely hard negatives, unlike monotonically increasing, saturated weights. The paper reports improved robustness with dynamic hard-negative sampling on three recommendation datasets; it does not establish the same benefit for masked BERT4Rec candidate cross-entropy. [Hard-BPR paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.19276v1).

For BERT4Rec with 16 uniform negatives, ordinary candidate cross-entropy already assigns negative gradients p_j=exp(s_j)/[exp(s_positive)+Σexp(s_k)]. Mathematical implication: adding detached hardness weights can duplicate that emphasis. If detached weights enter the denominator as w_j exp(s_j), even bounded, increasing w_j leaves exponential domination by extreme scores intact. If weighting separate losses, inspect w_j times each loss’s derivative. Saturation limits additional amplification; it does not establish preference for moderate competitors or false-negative robustness. A small uniform pool also limits available hard examples. Score-dependent weighting and detachment have clear precedent; novelty and effectiveness of a particular bounded rule require specification and controlled validation. Claims of moderate-negative emphasis need a demonstrably declining extreme-negative gradient, as in Hard-BPR.
